articleTitle: Can your server keep a secret?: If you're worried about cloud computers leaking data, help is on the way. But you might not like the performance
abstract: THE DESIGNERS of silicon chips have a lot to worry about. It can take months for a design to make it through the fab, and if things go wrong repairing any problems in the circuitry is a hugely expensive endeavour, not least because it costs millions just to make the intricate masks that print the design onto the silicon wafer. It is at the tape-out point that computing infrastructure becomes the crucial bottleneck.

articleTitle: Deep as chips: Artificial intelligence is appearing everywhere, but normal CPUs are not efficient platforms for the technology. Efficiency will only come with a new breed of microprocessors that are engineered specifically for the AI workload of the 2020s
abstract: THE GROWING USE of artificial intelligence (AI) is upscaling many standard types of IT workload as well as powering new services driven by advanced algorithmic data processing and machine learning techniques. Developers of AI systems, however, have been somewhat constrained by the limitations of standard microprocessors.

articleTitle: Let ai decide?
abstract: WOMEN WERE FINDING it tough to get jobs at Amazon. Not, it turned out, due to conscious discrimination in the HR department, but instead because of bias inherent in the AI-driven selection algorithm.

articleTitle: Storage gives boost to solar energy: The latest concentrated solar power projects, combined with energy storage, promise to make a significant contribution to the renewable energy effort
abstract: CONCENTRATED SOLAR technology systems use mirrors or lenses with tracking systems to focus a large area of sunlight onto a small area. These innovations, however, are far from new. In fact, legend has it, in 213 BC, Greek engineer Archimedes had set fire to Roman vessels attacking his home city with a giant mirror focusing the Sun's rays on the invaders. Today, they are used to provide industrial process heating or cooling, with excess thermal energy stored to generate electricity on demand. Quite the opposite to reducing ships to ashes, by far.

articleTitle: What's all the Buzz about? It may be what gave them their name, but it's what we hate most about them: Drones are a pain in the ears. The race is on, before they are pressed into service, to cure this device's greatest headache
abstract: IT'S PRETTY CLEAR that the age of drones is dawning. They are going to play an important role in the future - both in industrial and consumer worlds. In fact, within industry, drones are already successfully used. They are abundant in the entertainment industry for filming, and within the oil & gas and utilities industries for remote monitoring. With consumers, their use has mainly been recreational, but that's all about to change.

articleTitle: Turn it up! On trend at this year's CES were developments in the traditionally slow-moving medical electronics area of hearing aids. Yes, you heard right. The market is opening up and consumer electronics brands want a piece of the action
abstract: “WE CALL UNTREATED hearing loss the silent epidemic,” says Ruth Bridger, marketing director of Wear&Hear, just one of the many audio companies at this year's CES with new products for the hard of hearing. “Hearing connects us to people, and studies show that when you're not hearing properly you have a tendency to withdraw, become isolated, depressed; it can lead to cognitive decline and even dementia.”

articleTitle: 1871 That was the year that was…: As the IET starts its 150 year anniversary celebrations – a build-up that will conclude next year – we look at the events and technologies that made 1871 a landmark year for engineering
abstract: The year is 1871. Queen Victoria is on the throne and Liberal Prime Minister William Ewart Gladstone is head of the 20th Parliament of the United Kingdom. It is the year that rugby football is invented, Bank Holidays are created and trade unions legalised. Workers in Tyneside are striking for a shorter working day, while the completion of the transglobal London-Australia telegraph cable creates a landmark event in communications technology by uniting the opposite sides of the world. It is also the year that the Society of Telegraph Engineers is formed – the organisation that would become known as the IET. So, what was the state of engineering, what notable events shaped the world of technology during this year, and who were the main players?

articleTitle: A new holographic reality for business: A range of holographic and mixed-reality technologies promise to meet the challenges that businesses are facing in the wake of Covid-19
abstract: IMAGINE a future where, instead of attending a Zoom call to collaborate with your colleagues or clients, you could each generate accurate, full-size holograms of yourselves, which could be transmitted to a virtual replica of a site or office in real time.

articleTitle: When prosthetics meet aesthetics: Prosthetics by definition need to be functional, but can they be stylish as well? It seems the only limitation is imagination
abstract: I WAS HOLDING a disembodied foot — and my feelings about it were mixed. It was the end of a day shadowing in a prosthetics clinic. I'd sat in, quietly, on a consultation, then a fitting, then followed the prosthetist through to the workshop, where a pane of very strong, very hot acrylic was stretched by three technicians over a plaster cast of the patient's upper leg. I watched the small holes sawn into the plastic, into which were slotted the lengths of metal tubing that were cut to size and then fitted onto an incredibly technical (and incredibly expensive) knee joint. This, in turn, connected to a prosthetic lower leg, then to an ankle joint, then to a foot. The finished silhouette was — barring the skeletal pivots at the knee and ankle — perfectly human.

articleTitle: What happens when the raw materials run out?: The reserves of some rare earth minerals, used in electronics, medical equipment and renewable energy, could run out in less than 100 years
abstract: RARE EARTH MINERALS are naturally occurring resources, which cannot be recreated or replaced.

articleTitle: Gadgets: Smart tech improves a facemask, cycling, security, gardening, podcasting and more
The quest to end world hunger: Genetic engineering techniques could play an important role in ensuring the future of global food security
abstract: MANY COUNTRIES worldwide are facing the double burden of hunger and undernutrition alongside overweight and obesity, with one in three people across the globe currently suffering from some form of malnutrition. In fact, it's not unusual to find people with different forms of malnutrition living side-by-side.

articleTitle: Are the best universities producing the best engineers?: What does the perfect engineering graduate look like? It appears that UK universities might not always have the same understanding of this important question as engineering and technology companies
abstract: ACCORDING TO THE latest IET Skills and Demand Survey, not only are UK technology and engineering companies concerned about the well-documented engineering skills shortage but nearly three-quarters (73 per cent) of respondents say they have encountered candidates entering the job market with good academic knowledge but lacking the required practical work-related skills.

articleTitle: Stay in tune with a sonic miracle: Guitar music may not dominate in the way it once did, but guitars are still a billion-dollar industry with the strings that go on them a feat of engineering in their own right
abstract: WITH 2.5 MILLION UNITS sold annually in the US, and the UK pitching in with an extra 750,000, guitars are a billion-dollar business. Which means that the strings that go on them are big business too. If every new American and British six-string had their strings changed at the recommended frequency of once per month, they would in their first year alone consume sufficient length of metal wire to reach the 384,400km it takes to get to the Moon.

articleTitle: Contact app under scrutiny: Shortcomings in the NHSX contact-tracing app could limit its effectiveness and scare away users
abstract: E&T investigated concerns raised by computer engineers about timestamp and Google Analytics tracking. AT THE BEGINNING of May the open-source code of the NHS Covid-19 Android app beta version was uploaded to GitHub, a popular file-sharing platform. Since then developers have scrutinised every line of code and raised numerous issues on both its Android and iOS versions.

articleTitle: Our pick of CES
abstract: Sonarworks has used its experience in improving recording studios to build this impressive personal audio software for consumers. Headphones, like recording studios, all vary in how they treat the sound, especially between different manufacturers. Sound ID sets out to give you the best kind of sound for you, on any ordinary headphones.

articleTitle: Deep-sea treasures unlocked: Shipwrecks discovered in the Mediterranean have given scientists a tantalising glimpse into life along one of the world's most important trade routes, with underwater technology lending a helping hand
abstract: ADVANCES IN UNDERWATER technology are enabling a golden age of exploration and discovery in the deep ocean worldwide. The ‘Enigma Shipwrecks Project’ (ESP) in the eastern Mediterranean is no exception, uncovering no fewer than 12 shipwrecks sleeping under silty mud 2km below the surface in international waters off the coast of Lebanon. The team has found wrecks that span over two millennia from ancient Greek and Roman times to the last days of the Ottoman Empire.

articleTitle: Tough tests for covid-19: With a Covid-19 vaccination reckoned to be at least 18 months down the track, testing remains one of the most important options for combatting the pandemic
abstract: “WE HAVE A SIMPLE message for all countries. Test, test, test. Test every suspected case.” These are the words of Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, director-general of the World Health Organization (WHO), who in March 2020 declared the outbreak of respiratory disease Covid-19 to be a pandemic. Critical of international governmental response to the crisis, the public face of WHO said: “We have not seen an urgent enough escalation in testing, isolation and contact tracing, which is the backbone of the response. And to do that, you must test and isolate. You cannot fight the fire blindfolded.” Neither can significant inroads be made into arresting the pandemic, stressed Ghebreyesus, “if we don't know who is infected”.

articleTitle: How to party with netflix: I tried Netflix Party. The results were mixed but the experience was the reward. It brought me closer to self-quarantining loved-ones
abstract: THE CORONAVIRUS lockdown destroyed my social life. I am fairly lucky to have my wife who keeps me company. Others may not be so fortunate with no one at their side to share the burden of the plight. With more than a fifth of the global population under lockdown, it is only a matter of time until we see signs of the toll these protection measures have on people's mental health, especially those suffering from depression or similar.

articleTitle: Current thinking!: The workings of the human brain is still largely a mystery. Electrodes can offer an insight but some fear a sinister intent!
abstract: IN THE 1983 film ‘Brainstorm’, Christopher Walken and Natalie Wood develop a brain-computer interface (BCI) to read and process thoughts, which are then transferred to video tape to be shared with other people. This was used to share happy memories to reconcile the estranged pair, but also to experience a fellow scientist's heart attack, and it was the target of the military interest for torture and brainwashing.

articleTitle: Thie eccentric engineer
abstract: This month's edition tells the story of how mowing the lawn evolved from a task for an expert scythe-man to an 'amusing, useful and healthy exercise' for everyone.

articleTitle: Your letters
abstract: Following publication of the shocking figures for deaths and near misses on sections of the UK's smart motorways, several measures have been proposed including speeding up the response to breakdowns with radar monitoring and increasing the number of refuges. These measures will take time to implement and will still leave some broken-down vehicles at risk of high-speed collision.

articleTitle: Bizarre tech
abstract: Unveiled this year, for humorous or serious purposes, I can't quite decide, was Charmin's — that's right, the loo roll company — RollBot, a wee guy that brings you toilet paper using a smartphone app.

articleTitle: Bizarre Tech
abstract: Pet owners may be feeling guilty during this lockdown - you're home way too much and in their way all the time. So why not buy them a present that they'll probably despise?

abstract: From a retinal-imaging device that could detect Alzheimer's to a sand-conquering rover, here are the stories that make words like 'healthcare tech' and 'robotics' trend.

articleTitle: Your letters
abstract: Send your letters to The Editor, EST, Michael Faraday House, Six Hills Way, Stevenage, Herts SG1 2AY, UK, or to engtechletters@theiet.org. We reserve the right to edit letters and to use submissions in any other format.

articleTitle: Your letters
abstract: There's a lot of talk about heat-pump technology for domestic space and water heating, mainly as an alternative to natural gas. Systems using oil, LNG, electricity, coal and wood are also contenders for substitution, but the pros and cons vary considerably depending on which fuel is the basis of the comparison.

articleTitle: News Briefing: Space: Deep Space Network dish upgrade lets Nasa talk to Voyager 2 again
abstract: AFTER MONTHS of extensive upgrades to its Deep Space Network dish in Australia, Nasa has made contact once more with the Voyager 2 probe, which had been flying solo since March.

articleTitle: BizarreTech: Another month, another load of weird gadgets for you to ponder buying while stuck at home. This time, we have a smelly clock, a cosplay face mask and a board game designed for kitties
abstract: Sensory alarm clock Smell yourself awake. Sensorwake Trio is supposed to wake you up gently and “boost your mood every morning” by “stimulating” three of your senses: smell, sight and sound.

articleTitle: BuzzWords: VR 3D printing cyber ai drones cyber security: From army applications to stalking fruit flies and mosquitoes, here are stories that make words like ‘drones’ and ‘robotics’ trend
abstract: Flying insects have developed effective strategies for navigating in natural environments. But studies on these strategies are a challenge for scientists because of how tiny they are and quick when in flight. The only time researchers can study such creatures is when they're “tethered”.

articleTitle: Diversity: “I've done so much, and there's still so much more to do…”: Dr Shini Somara talks to Dr Marlene Kanga, Past President of the World Federation of Engineering Organisations, and a keen advocate for inclusivity in engineering
abstract: AUSTRALIAN engineer Dr Marlene Kanga AM FTSE HonFIEAust HonFIChemE is the immediate Past President of the World Federation of Engineering Organisations (WFEO), representing 100 nations and some 30 million engineers. With a background in chemical engineering, she is now a keen advocate for the promotion of diverse and inclusive groups within engineering around the world, and here expands on a topic that is very close to her heart.

articleTitle: AfterAll: Travel may you never need the services of a ‘Horizontal Travel Agent‘: As the continuing ‘Covid War’ keeps millions of people away from travel, our columnist reviews his readers' techno-travel reveries
abstract: IT IS NICE to see our lives getting back to normal after the pandemic, slowly but surely (or so I hope). Alas, so far, the ‘Covid War’ — not to be confused with the Cold War — is still raging in many parts of the world. There is one striking similarity between the two ‘wars’: they both impose heavy restrictions on our freedom of movement and travel.

articleTitle: Buzz words: Lovesick social media: From getting over an ex to garments on a baby you probably wish you had with your ex. Here are the stories that make words like ‘social media’ and ‘wearables’ trend
abstract: Stay off the internet if you want to get over your ex!: Imagine scrolling through your Facebook feed to find that your ex, who you were with for five years, is now 'in a relationship'? Or better yet, the 'memories' feature shows you a sweet photo of you and your ex on a Hawaiian beach? I can imagine you'd be pretty bummed out about seeing these things. But don't you fret, you're not the only one. In fact, a new University of Colorado Boulder study has found that these feelings of sadness are not uncommon, and that getting over a break-up is a lot harder in the digital age.

articleTitle: Dear evil engineer: Question could i crush my enemies with a giant robot suit?: A villain's plan for vengeance by mecha violates a fundamental rule of engineering: Avoid overcomplication
abstract: Dear Evil Engineer; I'm short and socially awkward with a receding jawline. I'm 24 years old and I've never killed an enemy, or even threatened one without them laughing at me. I'm an outcast. It's not fair.

articleTitle: ViewFrom Brussels: Energy hydrogen and nuclear play the EU waiting game: Will EU countries agree on which ‘green’ projects are best suited to propelling them out of this economic slump?
abstract: IN SETTING UP a level playing field for green finance, the EU put together a common rulebook, known as the taxonomy, which tells investors whether or not their money is tied up in a sustainable project.

articleTitle: After all: Transport i am not a train – a guided walk inside the Eurotunnel: In an attempt to make history, our columnist boards the Eurostar post-Brexit
abstract: “WHAT A WORLD of passengers on our steamer! Princes, dukes, gentlemen, ladies, tailors, milliners, people of every rank and calling, all jumbled together. The power of steam is not confined to material objects… Steam is a great democratic power of our age; annihilating the conventional distinctions, differences, and social distance between man and man, as well as the natural distances between place and place.”

articleTitle: The eccentric engineer: A tale of six pips — how the BBC became the national arbiter of time
abstract: EVERY ENGINEER needs to know the time, if only so as to not miss lunch. Since 1924 many Britons have been checking their watches against the BBC time signal, known affectionately as ‘the pips’.

articleTitle: Editor's letter: From facial recognition to body-worn cameras, technology is useful but controversial in the fight against crime
abstract: TECHNOLOGY has the potential to improve most areas of life and in some it can save lives. But where it is a matter of life and death is also where it has to be applied with the most care. Policing, detection and enforcement is one such area. We all want to stop crime and catch criminals but without discrimination, harassment or a police state.

articleTitle: Dear Evil Engineer: Question Can I replace my useless henchmen with robot guards?: A villain is sick of their plans being compromised by hopeless henchmen. Could they be replaced with autonomous systems?
abstract: Dear Evil Engineer, The henchmen who guard my facilities are a liability. I employ two dozen beefy men who couldn't shoot a barn door, and consistently lose fist fights with hopelessly outnumbered do-gooders trying to interfere with my schemes. The final straw came when three of my guards were knocked out with blows to the head and had their uniforms and passes stolen by a gang of meddlers, who then impersonated them to gain access to my server room and disrupt a scheme I had been working on for months

articleTitle: Bizarre Tech: In these weird times, some people want to move their mod cons outdoors. Some lose perspective on personal hygiene. And some just want something stupid on their face. There's tech for all of them
abstract: Electricity-generating barbeque: Charge your phone with cooking You want a barbeque with a USB charger? You got it, buddy.

articleTitle: Editor's letter
abstract: SONIC ARRIVES on the big screen this month after 30 years battling Robotnik on the small screen and, indeed, the very small screen. While it may be outside his comfort zone, it's not really a bigger pond for the little blue hedgehog. The games industry was the new kid on the block back then, but today it's bigger than the movie and music industries combined.

articleTitle: Editor's Letter: Activists raise awareness, but it's engineers who are working to overcome the world's environmental challenges
abstract: REMEMBER Extinction Rebellion or XR and their direct action on our city streets? It seems like an age ago but it was only six months. Covid-19 pushed climate change down the public agenda for a while, although I started to receive press releases promoting the idea of a sustainable post-pandemic economic recovery back in the summer. Now everyone it seems is talking about it. Boris Johnson jumped on the bandwagon with a ‘green recovery’ speech. Prince William and David Attenborough launched a £50m prize scheme for innovation that ought to appeal to our readers (p9).

articleTitle: ViewFrom Manchester: Social media will ads boycott bump ‘arrogant’ Facebook into hate speech action?: Social media has run out of time on hate speech
abstract: AS I WRITE, more than 900 companies have joined a July-long advertising boycott of Facebook. It calls on the social media company to take far greater steps to stop the spread of hate speech across its network.

articleTitle: Buzz words
abstract: Call this a ‘biotechnological’ breakthrough if you may, but for the first time, researchers have successfully reproduced the electrical properties of biological neurons onto semiconductor chips. And according to its creators, these artificial neurons could pave the way for future medical devices to cure chronic diseases such as heart failure, Alzheimer's, and other diseases of neuronal degeneration.

articleTitle: The Eccentric Engineer: Perhaps we shouldn't be so hard on the futurists: This edition of Eccentric Engineer tells many stories of the thankless job of predicting the engineered future. Unfortunately, everyone gets it wrong from time to time
abstract: PART OF BEING an engineer is the ability to predict the future – not in a mystical, crystal ball sort of way, but gauging what might be needed, what solutions to current problems might look like and, to a degree, critiquing those developments as they appear.

articleTitle: View from brussels: Pandemic introducing the eu ‘e-summit’ during coronavirus outbreak: Coronavirus is wreaking havoc on how the EU institutions go about their day-to-day business, not to mention long-term planning
abstract: THE EU'S INITIAL response to the virus scare was a rather disjointed affair. The European Commission, Council and Parliament – the three main institutions -all started implementing different in-house measures to try and contain the disease.

articleTitle: After All: Literature: Cheered up by a Munchausen of the space era: To beat the ennui of the partial lockdown, our columnist opens a virtual book club for E&T readers and would love for you to join the conversation
abstract: LET'S FACE IT: Covid-19 is not going away any time soon, and the only thing we can do under the circumstances is to keep living our lives as close to normal as possible.

articleTitle: View from: Brussels: The UK's membership of the European Union ended on 31 January: Now for the talks. In 11 months, when they end, the UK-EU border could look very different
abstract: BREXIT ‘PHASE 1’ is done. Now to flesh out the nature of Britain's relationship with Brussels before the ‘phase 2’ end-of-year deadline. All manner of trade, technology and energy issues will be affected, depending on whether the UK government insists on breaking with EU rules or sticks closely to them in return for lucrative unfettered market access.

articleTitle: Money + markets: While traders react emotionally to the spread of the virus, causing price volatility, Bitcoin is the new digital equivalent of gold
abstract: THE MARKET is meant to be a perfect judge of all information so that the price of any instrument is right all the time, every time.

articleTitle: View From Manchester: Politics It's still the system, Rishi, and it does need repeating: Despite all the good Rishi Sunak has done, his efforts need to show more thought and transparency
abstract: RISHI SUNAK, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, is the pollsters' pick for the most popular politician in the UK right now, but how much store should we set by a smart suit, polished delivery and – of course – a firehose of public money?

articleTitle: Dear evil engineer
abstract: A villain wonders what they will ever do with their impulse purchase of a barrel of assorted nuclear waste. Dear Evil Engineer, During lockdown I've been coping with cabin fever by ordering lots of rubbish that I don't need. Having decided to stop buying from Amazon on ethical grounds, I went on the dark web and bought 100 compromised Uber Eats accounts, enough ketamine to knock out a plesiosaur, and a barrel of 'High Quality Random Selection Best in UK' nuclear waste. While the Uber Eats accounts and narcotics will make quarantine more enjoyable, I'm now questioning my decision to purchase the radioactive material. I have done minimal field work as a villain beyond a few factfinding trips, and have no experience handling dangerous substances. What am I going to do with it? Yours, A regretful villain

articleTitle: View from Brussels: COVID-19 no Island is an Island: How the EU's virus fund affects the UK
abstract: EVERY ONE OF the EU's now-27 members is due to see a dip in GDP this year because of the Covid-19's huge impact on productivity That is why the bloc has scrambled to chart a course out of the pandemic-induced slump.

articleTitle: View From Brussels: Election transatlantic ties at a junction as the EU aims for self-sufficiency: US-EU relations are tense amid a presidential election campaign and ongoing pandemic. Where do the two sides stand on digital, energy and tech issues?
abstract: DEPENDING ON WHO emerges triumphant after November's poll – incumbent Donald Trump or Joe Biden – ties between the US and Europe could either sour further or start to enjoy a resurgence. In some cases, it won't matter who wins the White House.

articleTitle: Money & Markets: Economy governments are running a financial engineering experiment: The global economy is in shock thanks to coronavirus lockdowns, and governments are implementing innovations that could serve as potential rescue packages. Huge changes are coming, and that brings opportunity to those positioned to take advantage
abstract: WHEN ENGINEERS BUILT the cathedrals of Europe, erecting their buildings to God's glory, they didn't exactly know whether their designs would work. Economics is in that state today. With governments building up mountains of debt, too many of these structures seem as likely to fall as the walls of Notre Dame, without their ad hoc flying buttresses.

articleTitle: Bizarre tech: You think a national lockdown would dampen my spirits and prevent me from lightly mocking the latest tech? You are so very wrong
abstract: Rotofarm: Your veggies spin me right round, baby… Looking like a giant running wheel for large rodents, Rotofarm is the latest product by Australian biotechnology company Bace.

articleTitle: Editor's letter: Consumer choice is making itself felt in healthcare, from custom prosthetics to everyday activity monitors
abstract: ONE OF THE IMPORTANT trends at the recent CES 2020 consumer electronics showcase in Las Vegas was the proliferation of health and medical exhibits.

articleTitle: After all: Railways the soviet version of a driverless vodka train: From the comfort of his house, our temporarily ‘isolated’ columnist recounts his scariest and most incredible techno travel story
abstract: FOR A COMPULSIVE traveller like myself, suffering since childhood with a severe case of dromomania – a medically described irrepressible passion for purposeless travel, or ‘a travelling fugue’ – being stuck at home as a ‘high-risk case’ for at least three months due to a pandemic, or for any other reason, is almost physically painful. I am sure that many E&T readers must also be feeling claustrophobic.

articleTitle: View from Brussels: This year will be a testing ground for all the EU's major policies
abstract: THE UK WILL cease to be a fully-fledged EU member on 31 January but that is by no means the end of the Brexit saga. Negotiating the exit deal was, after all, meant to be the easiest part. Now comes the agreement on future relations.

Remember when everything revolved around higher or lower interest rates? When the economy slumped, down would come interest rates to make it grow faster. When the economy was seen to be overheating, up they would go, and down would go the economy. It was a blunt instrument designed to inflict pain on borrowers and thereby cramp their ability to drive demand. Less demand, less inflation.

abstract: HISTORY IS WRITTEN by the victors, or at least it's written about the victors, and this column is as guilty of that as any other. The Brunels, Teslas and Leonardos of this world were undoubtedly brilliant and tenacious, but they were lucky. There have been other engineers who have worked just as hard, perhaps with just as much vision, but perhaps the dice simply never landed well for them. This month's column is a tribute to them and particularly the unluckiest engineers of all.

Interview: Words and portrait by Nick Smith: With more than a thousand patents to his name, technology advocate Dean Kamen, inventor of the Segway, is one of the most influential innovators of his generation. But innovation and invention are two very different things, he says
abstract: AS ALL the technology history books will tell you, Dean Kamen, president of DEKA Research & Development Corporation, New Hampshire, US, is best known for inventing the Segway. In the two decades since it hit the market, the ‘electric, self-balancing human transporter’ has become ubiquitous, finding uses in virtually any pedestrian application where there is a need that sits in the gap between walking and requiring a golf-cart. You see them in airports. They're used as police patrol vehicles. They're used in sports, tourism, broadcast, security, mobile rescue, logistics… the list goes on. But, as his transporter turns 20, Kamen doesn't want to be known just as the ‘Segway guy’, unless you talk about what (for him) is the invention's real application: the gyroscopic technology underpinning the iBot self-balancing wheelchair that he describes as “a mobility system restoring freedom and dignity”.

articleTitle: Interview jean page: In three decades at BAE Systems, principal technologist Jean Page has seen sweeping changes in engineering. Innovation, once dominated by the defence industry, now relies on collaboration with the medical and gaming industries
abstract: “I COULD PICK out technologies that are going to be the next great thing,” says Jean Page. “But the biggest thing we're seeing now is the rate of change of technology.” Page, who is the principal technologist at BAE Systems Air Sector, says this rapidity is creating an environment in which “we need to spot a technology, to seize it and put it into an application along timescales we've never seen before. We need to look beyond the boundaries of our disciplines, which is where the data analytics and machine learning is really going to help us, because it's hard to spot opportunities without the knowledge, network and experience.”

articleTitle: Book Reviews the world according to physics, the bridge, robert paul and the origins of british cinema: Princeton university press ‘the world according to physics‘: Science fundamentals with a sense of fun, the geopolitics of energy, and the man who launched the British film industry
abstract: BY JIM AL-KHALILI, £12.99, ISBN 9780691182308: The problem facing anyone attempting to bring physics to a lay audience, says Jim Al-Khalili at the beginning of ‘The World According to Physics’, is that the entire enterprise is pretty much doomed from the word go. The reason for this is that the research scientists who write the brilliant academic papers aren't always good at communicating ideas to a non-scientific audience, while those with the communication skills – so-called ‘popular science’ authors – are not necessarily always in total command of the complexity, scale and subtleties of their subject.

articleTitle: TheBiggerPicture boom supersonic XB-1
abstract: In October, aerospace company Boom Supersonic unveiled its one-third-scale demonstrator, the XB-1, vaunted as the world's first independently developed supersonic jet. XB-1 is scheduled to fly for the first time in 2021, and will undergo a 100 per cent carbon-neutral flight-test programme. Boom's innovations include one of the highest-efficiency civil supersonic engine intakes ever tested. This will, the company hopes, deliver a breakthrough in propulsive efficiency and prepare the air for Overture – a 55-passenger supersonic transport with 8,300km of range – which is proposed to be introduced in 2029. Boom's XB-1 virtual rollout highlighted some of the aircraft's notable features: XB-1's 26.8m-long fuselage has been optimally shaped for high-speed aerodynamic efficiency, and its carbon-composite airframe maintains its strength and rigidity, even under the high temperatures and stresses of supersonic flight. Three J85–15 engines, designed by General Electric, provide around 55kN of thrust, allowing XB-1 to fly at breakthrough supersonic speeds.

articleTitle: Interview
abstract: One of the digital era's most exciting innovators, social entrepreneur Charles Adler is best known as co-founder of Kickstarter, the crowdfunding platform that for a decade has changed the way new ideas are brought to market. WATCHING CHARLES Adler present to a hall full of devotees is a bit like experiencing a mash-up of an Apple press conference and a U2 concert. He's clad in the American tech guru's uniform of boom mic and skinny black jeans. Using the whole stage, he prowls in front of a backdrop of revolving slogan projections reminding the audience that “rules are meant to be broken” and innovation “comes from the fringe". He switches between evangelising directly to the audience and talking to himself, locked in a bubble of self-belief that is frightening in its intensity. One thing is certain, and that is you walk away from a Charles Adler presentation 'on message'. You might not know what every word of his hyper-trendy 'Wired-speak' idiolect actually means, but you are left in absolutely no doubt that it's important. This is the word of the man who kickstarted Kickstarter, the man whose next project is so ambitious and so veiled in secrecy that its success seems to be inevitable.

articleTitle: The measure of cessna eCaravan: The world's largest all-electric aircraft recently made a successful maiden flight over Washington state, engine manufacturer magniX announced
abstract: A SOLO TEST PILOT took off in the nineseater plane and flew over the AeroTEC Flight Test Center at Moses Lake, Washington, followed by a small chase plane on 28 May. The electric aircraft took off and climbed to 2,500ft before cruising around over the facility for more than 20 minutes. Commentators said it was “barely making any noise”, with a much smaller Cessna chase plane “twice as loud”.

articleTitle: Interview: Words and portrait by Nick Smith: Nobel laureate and director of the Francis Crick Institute, geneticist Sir Paul Nurse discusses his pioneering work in cell research and why the UK simply wasn't ready for coronavirus, despite “being able to predict it”
abstract: THE “TRAGEDY” of coronavirus is that “we could have predicted that we were bound to have pandemics”. What's more, says Sir Paul Nurse, with world travel connecting the global population of 7.8 billion “easily and quickly”, and with a projected increase to 10 billion by the year 2050, “we are bound to have more. New organisms – particularly viruses, but also bacteria – will travel rapidly around the world.” All of this is obvious, says Nurse, whose new book ‘What is Life?‘ has just been published. When it comes to our current health crisis, “with coronavirus we could have been so much better prepared”.

articleTitle: Book Reviews: Online Afterlives, Analogia, Sealand: Death-defying technology, the shifting nature of humanity, and the story of a micronation
abstract: ‘Analogia’ is an odd book. Author and historian of technology George Dyson weaves together autobiography, science and 300 years of history into a sprawling exploration of how technology, nature and humanity have shaped each other and will shape each other in years to come.

abstract: As countries around the world grapple with the Covid-19 pandemic, Toronto-based VYZR Technologies has released an innovative type of personal protective pquipment (PPE) that shields the wearer's face and filters their air.

abstract: IT IS UNLIKELY that the world will meet its 2050 net zero carbon climate goals without a major acceleration in clean energy innovation, the International Energy Agency has warned.

abstract: THE COVID-19 PANDEMIC triggered a bout of changes to local cycling infrastructure as commuters eschewed public transport. Enthusiasm to support cyclists all across Europe led to a whopping �1bn splurge into measures such as car-free sections, cycle lanes, traffic-calming and reduction zones, and wider pavements.

articleTitle: The Measure Of The Candela Seven: An electric-powered hydrofoil speedboat that reduces energy consumption, noise and seasickness by ‘flying’ above the waves made an appearance on lakes in Switzerland last month
abstract: THE ELECTRIC BOAT, called the Candela Seven, can hit speeds of 55km/h when its foils lift it out of the water. Its Swedish manufacturer, Candela, say it travels further and more smoothly than other electric boats.

articleTitle: TheGraphic Apple's supply chain evolution: A visual analysis shows how Apple's supplier network has evolved over past years, and what these changes mean for the tech giant's future and competition
abstract: APPLE announced in June that it will begin making its own chips, confirming insider predictions of a move away from Intel chip dependence. CEO Tim Cook said the company will produce processors for its own desktops and laptops, which marks a big strategic shift.

articleTitle: Book reviews: Stealth, land of wondrous cold, in praise of folly
abstract: Stealth aircraft, Antarctic science and the strange beliefs of the otherwise brilliant. If ever there was a geographical region that unites humanity's twin obsessions with terrestrial exploration and the advancement of science, it is the continent of Antarctica. And if ever there was a book on precisely that relationship it is 'Land of Wondrous Cold', in which Gillen D'Arcy Wood describes the unfolding drama of the White Continent's role in plate tectonics, climate change and species evolution, stretching back into deep-time history.

articleTitle: How to live when nobody dies: Three score and ten is so 1970s. Today, the average baby born in the UK will live long enough to see the beginning of the 22nd century. Increasingly we also hear claims of longevity breakthroughs that could propel those children – and maybe even their parents – into triple digits and beyond. But is eternal life something we want outside of science fiction? And how will society cope if it is?
abstract: “THE FIRST ten million years were the worst,” said Marvin. “The second ten million years, they were the worst too. The third ten million years I didn't enjoy at all. After that I went into a bit of a decline.”

abstract: How much can a book tell you about a pandemic when we are still in the midst of it, with knowledge about the virus, the disease it causes, and its aftereffects building day by day? As it turns out, more than enough to justify its publication.

abstract: THERE WAS A TIME when arriving at a petrol station was part of the romance of driving. Many of them were even stylish examples of contemporary design.

articleTitle: TheBiggerPicture Socially distanced tram
abstract: An Italian design firm has come up with the idea of a tram that enables social distancing. Architect Arturo Tedeschi of A>T teamed up with fellow designer Lorenzo Pio Cocco to create Passerella, a vehicle specifically designed for the city of Milan. The city has been one of the worst hit by Italy's Covid-19 epidemic, and the tram will cater for citizens' changing habits postcoronavirus. With Milan's yellow tram a treasured symbol of public transport, the project also references the iconic 1503 model by reinterpreting its style and proportions with novel technologies.

articleTitle: News: The Graphic Forest fire-fighting: California's latest fires show that rich western developed nations lack the technology to battle blazes. There is a pressing need for new approaches
abstract: THIS HAS BEEN a bad year for wildfires in California. A month before the official wildfire season started, more than 2.5 million acres (10,000km<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>) burned prematurely. articleTitle: The gallery: World's first online graduation: Students at Business Breakthrough University in Tokyo didn't get a traditional ceremony, but had the next best thing using ‘newme’ telepresensence robots and a tablet
abstract: A Japanese University has held the world's first online graduation ceremony using ‘newme’ telepresensence robots and a tablet hosting a Zoom call. Business Breakthrough University graduates had the experience of accepting their diplomas at the Hotel Grand Palace in Tokyo, virtually on 28 March 2020. Professor Shugo Yanaka, Dean of Global Business Administration, said: “We hope this initiative will be helpful to educational institutions who are having difficulty holding ceremonies.”

articleTitle: News: Transport Self-driving cars could be legal on UK roads by early 2021
abstract: THE UK government has launched a consultation that could pave the way for self-driving cars to be introduced on roads as early as next year. The Department for Transport has issued a call for evidence for the ‘Automated Lane Keeping System’ – an automated system that can take over control of a vehicle at low speeds, keeping it in its present lane on motorways.

articleTitle: Book interview: Starting up outside silicon valley: We're moving away from the entrenched idea that successful tech start-ups need to have their roots in San Francisco says author Alexandre Lazarow, whose new book examines the emergence of global innovation frontiers
abstract: “WHEN MY students ask me 'what should I build?' or 'what sort of start-up should I be doing?' I respond by asking them what their motivation is in the first place,” says Alexandre Lazarow. Invariably, he notes, the answer to these questions will be an expression of creating a force for good. “They want to make an impact, generate jobs and wealth for their ecosystems. That's what drives them. That's what drives entrepreneurship. It's not just the launching of new products. It's the impact that it has on society.”

articleTitle: The measure of perseverance mars rover: Nasa has chosen a name for its next Mars rover, Perseverance, which is scheduled to launch in July and join the eminent Curiosity on the Red Planet in 2021
abstract: THE US SPACE agency has announced the name of its Mars 2020 rover, following a six-month competition that drew more than 28,000 entries from American students in kindergarten through to high school.

articleTitle: Book interview: Mathematics' greatest hits
abstract: ADAM HART-DAVIS is quick to admit that for many people “maths is very difficult”, a problem he attributes to the way in which the subject is taught in schools today. “A teacher says: ‘So, the area of a circle is pi times the square of the radius. Has everyone got that?’ Of course, everyone's completely mystified, but they nod and say yes to the teacher, and so the teacher moves on.” Once you've missed that point, says Hart-Davis, “you're going to be hopelessly left behind. The result is that most of us grow up mathematically inept and we never get to love it. You need a rather special brain to cope with mathematics.”

articleTitle: Space Training: The Bigger Picture Moon landings in 2024
abstract: Teams at Nasa's Johnson Space Center in Texas are testing tools and training for operations on the Moon, as part of the Artemis programme to land the first woman and next man on the lunar south pole in 2024. In this picture, astronauts are demonstrating the exploration spacesuit in the Neutral Buoyancy Lab and engineers in ‘hard hat’ dive equipment are simulating tasks the crew might perform on the Moon.

articleTitle: Book interview: The end of the great acceleration?: From the prevalence of digital data to national economies, everything is slowing down, and not just because of the Covid-19 pandemic. Danny Dorling's new book ‘Slowdown’ has the maths and statistics to prove it
abstract: “ABOUT SIX years ago I began measuring as many things about human progress as I could measure, expecting to find that half of them were accelerating while the other half were slowing down.” Danny Dorling is explaining why he chose to write his new book – ‘Slowdown’ – at a time when even the experts, including himself, were seeing a confused picture of progress in a digitally supercharged world.

articleTitle: Thinking cap: New Year, new puzzles to exercise your brain. This month, computer science, magical numbers and lots of bunnies are here to test your mind
abstract: Alice and Bob fell in love while studying computer science together. They love computers and are the sort of people who think it's romantic that computers use a number system that is base two (1s and 0s).

articleTitle: The graphic nuclear stockpiles
abstract: THERE WERE 13,865 nuclear weapons on the planet last time anyone counted. A quarter of them are, in one way or another, deployed with operational forces. Russia holds the most, with 6,500, according to 2018 figures, and has been upgrading nuclear storage sites. Various emerging superpowers appear eager to increase their nuclear defence capabilities - a dangerous cocktail in times of turmoil.

abstract: Plastic is a massive problem in our world and every year, over 900 million toothpaste tubes enter landfills and oceans across the world.

articleTitle: The Bigger Picture: Smart Contact Lens
abstract: A Californian start-up called Mojo Vision claims to have developed the world's first true smart contact lens, which puts a screen against your eye to display information. Named Mojo Lens, the working prototype has a built-in display that gives the wearer useful information without “forcing them to look down at a screen or losing focus on the people and the world around them”. Mojo says its Invisible Computing platform enables information to be instantaneous, unobtrusive and hands-free. The company holds patents critical to the development of an augmented-reality (AR) smart contact lens, and is looking for business partners to develop the idea. An early application of the product would help people struggling with low vision by providing real-time contrast and lighting enhancements, as well as zoom functionality.

articleTitle: Words and portrait by Nick Smith: Strategy director at the University of Liverpool's Materials Innovation Factory Matt Reed is spearheading a project to harness Industry 4.0 to create 'Covid-19-resilient virtual laboratories' for both academic research and industrial R&D
abstract: “LOCKDOWN WAS really interesting in the way it affected the way different people worked,” says Matt Reed. “Office workers decamped, set up at home, downloaded Zoom and just got on with it. No new technology was required for that. All the things they needed were on their laptops. But it had a big impact on the way these organisations did their work. There are businesspeople I know that are already cancelling their office leases because they just don't need office space to run their businesses anymore. Offices? Done.”

articleTitle: The bigger picture hyper realistic wave simulation
abstract: A giant virtual wave crashes against a glass box in an epic art installation in South Korea. The vivid installation, which appears on Seoul's SMTown COEX building, South Korea's biggest digital billboard, is described as an ‘anamorphic illusion‘. Appearing for exactly one minute every hour, the simulation is extremely realistic. Titled ‘Wave’, the project was designed by d'strict, a firm specialising in immersive technology to create public art. The project took four months to complete, but social media was divided. One user compared it to the inside of a washing machine while another, perhaps with an eye on the current Covid-19 restrictions, mused that it was a “self-quarantined sea“. The screen is 80×20m and is usually a platform for advertisements and pop videos.

articleTitle: What the Victorians have done for us: Climate change, congestion and poor land management are modern-day challenges. But who got us into this state? Could it be the Victorians?
abstract: “WE'VE GOT the car, airplane and electric telegraph so we could talk from one side of the world to the other. We've got railways speeding all over the country and exported them worldwide. The technology was unstoppable. They were a remarkable set of people.”

articleTitle: The measure of pooley bridge: The UK's first stainless steel road bridge of its kind is expected to open for traffic in the coming weeks
abstract: CUMBRIA COUNTY Council announced that its £5m project at Pooley Bridge in the Eden District will hit its key milestone soon, after work resumed on the bridge at the end of April following a brief suspension due to the coronavirus pandemic. The main span was built in sections off-site and then assembled next to the river. It will be lifted into place by a crawler crane.

articleTitle: After all: Wandering lost and nostalgic in the world's most liveable city
abstract: LIKE THE alcoholic protagonist of V Yerofeev's famous novella “Moscow-Petushki” (“Moscow Stations”) who, having wandered around central Moscow for years, could never find the Kremlin, I had been unable — no matter how hard I tried — to spot the Danube while in Vienna last December.

articleTitle: Not just the carbon emissions: The effects of carbon emissions are well known, yet scientists argue we need a more comprehensive approach for assessing and guiding humanity's environmental impact. We investigate how the concept of Planetary Boundaries could inform how engineers work
abstract: WHEN COVID-19 lockdowns were announced earlier this year, the global economy ground to a painful halt. However, one unintended beneficiary was the environment. Carbon emissions plummeted, air pollution dissipated, usually murky rivers ran clear and there were countless good news stories from all over the world of resurgent wildlife.

articleTitle: A quiet place
abstract: With levels of road transport, air travel and industrial output lessening dramatically during the Covid-19 lockdown, one side-effect has been a reduction in noise pollution. But there's more to 'global quieting' than being able to hear more birds. ACCORDING TO the World Health Organization, noise affects over 100 million people in Europe alone. Exposure to chronic noise pollution not only causes obvious problems such as hearing loss and sleep deprivation, but is also linked to high blood pressure, heart disease and cognitive impairment in children. Road traffic noise is said to contribute to at least 12,000 premature deaths annually in Europe, amounting to a loss of 1.6 million high-quality-life days. The European Environment Agency (EEA) has found that the same number of children are experiencing either learning difficulties or disruptions due to excessive aircraft noise.

articleTitle: The graphic infection risk among engineers: Data suggests there is a lower risk of people in engineering roles being exposed to disease and infections, but outliers do exist
abstract: WHEN IT COMES to being exposed to disease and infections, being a nurse or a GP, for example, will put you at greater risk than those in an engineering role. This sounds accurate, but during the current Covid-19 pandemic E&T has scrutinised various occupations in the engineering and technology sector to discover how exposed workers are to the risk to contracting and spreading an infectious virus.

articleTitle: Words and portrait by Nick Smith: Ricardo CEO Dave Shemmans says that in order to adapt to the challenges facing industry in a post-Covid landscape we need to get back to addressing fundamental megatrends such as climate change, pollution and resource scarcity
abstract: EVERYONE THESE DAYS is having meetings over digital platforms such as Zoom and Teams. It's becoming part of the much-trumpeted new reality. Yet for Dave Shemmans, holding meetings this way isn't just a makeshift response to not being able to meet in person. For the CEO of global engineering and environmental consultancy Ricardo, it's something that we should be embracing. It's a way of taking fewer flights, spending less time in the car, reducing the environmental impact of doing business. If you can save time, money and the planet by plugging into this simple measure, it becomes a ‘no-brainer’ rather than an inconvenience brought about by government-mandated working from home.

articleTitle: AI future-proofs power network: An award-winning project is having a positive impact on the Scottish electricity network
abstract: A GOOD TEST OF the worthiness of an award winner comes from revisiting that project further into its working life. Will the water that has passed under the bridge wash away the gloss? That is certainly not the case with the Networks Constraints Early Warning System (NCEWS), which won the 2019 E&T Innovation of the Year at the IET's annual Innovation Awards.

articleTitle: Space uk considers scrapping homegrown satellite navigation system
abstract: BRITAIN'S PROPOSED satellite navigation system, which was intended to be an alternative to Europe's Galileo system, may be scrapped for being a waste of taxpayer funds. The Telegraph reported earlier this month that civil servants in both the Cabinet Office and Department for Business are pushing ministers to announce the project's cancellation.

articleTitle: On screen: 10 tech villains and 10 heroes: As an array of hero and villain films hit cinemas this year, including the much-anticipated (but unfortunately delayed) James Bond, we look at film and TV's all-time best baddies and goodies
abstract: ENGINEERING AND technology have generally got a bum rap from the movies and TV, but not always. Here are the best exceptions: ten each of baddies and goodies.

articleTitle: The measure of copernicus sentinel-6 michael freilich: As part of Europe's Copernicus programme, the Sentinel-6 radar altimetry reference mission will extend the investigation of sea-surface height measurements until at least 2030
abstract: SEA-LEVEL RISE is one of the most severe consequences of climate change. The rate at which oceans are rising has accelerated over the past 25 years, and scientists expect it to speed up in the years to come. To be able to keep a closer eye on sea levels, permanent observations over the world's oceans are needed.

articleTitle: BookReviews: The Sirens of Mars, The Chemical Reaction, Calling Bullsh!t: A personal take on space exploration, the return of a fictional engineer, and a primer in spotting misinformation
abstract: Hot on the heels of last year's ‘The Chemical Detective’ comes the second in what every engineer must hope is going to be a long series of thrillers concerning the adventures of Jaq Silver, chemical engineer. If you enjoyed the Chernobyl-based first instalment, Fiona Erskine's follow-up — ‘The Chemical Reaction’ — is even better.

articleTitle: Book interview: Not just gazing into space: Our day jobs have changed to the point that today routine tasks are being done by computers, while the thinking – or ‘invisible work’ – is reserved for humans. Author John Howkins explains why this can create big problems
abstract: IT WAS ALFRED NOBEL who said, “If I have a thousand ideas and only one turns out to be good, I am satisfied”. While we can agree that it all worked out fine for the Swedish engineer – his name immortalised in his eponymous prize – a statistician might say that by Nobel's own admission he seemed to be content with not putting 99.9 per cent of his time to proper use. Welcome to the world of ‘invisible work’, the theme and title of John Howkins' latest, which examines what we're doing with all that ‘downtime’ and its implications for today's workplace.

articleTitle: ThinkingCap: Puzzle 1 sharing a birthday: Birthdays, matchsticks and letters are on the menu this month, with a chance of a prize for the correct answer
abstract: The party was going well. Animated chatter sparkled across the large room, which was filled with several dozen people.

articleTitle: Book Interview: The universe and our place in it: It's a big subject and an even bigger place. Yet somehow Professor Andrew Newsam manages to explain the mysteries of the universe in a brief and entertaining read
abstract: If you ever thought that the universe was one of those big, complex, hard-to-conceptualise topics that is best left to those specialist scientists in their world of unfeasibly large telescopes, then you�re not alone. It stands to reason that when you have a subject so vast that once it goes beyond what science can tell us it strays into philosophy, you might have something of a challenge on your hands when it comes to explaining the whole thing in one slim volume.

articleTitle: Book interview
abstract: CONVENTIONAL WISDOM, for what it's worth, has long held that video games are to blame for pretty much everything that's wrong with society. They encourage violence, isolate gamers in lonely digital silos, narrow our minds and rob us of leisure time that could be so much better spent climbing trees, fishing and playing football. Of course, we've got the hyperactive red-top media to blame for never letting the truth get in the way of a good story. But what is the truth about video games? What does this picture look like when we go behind the headlines and take a long, hard, dispassionate look at the scientific research and data?

articleTitle: News: E&T reveals shortlist of finalists for innovation awards 2020
abstract: THE SHORTLIST for the E&T Innovation Awards 2020 has been announced, celebrating people, projects and organisations revolutionising our world with excellence in engineering and technology. The Awards give global recognition to those creating innovative and creative solutions, which are delivering a return – whether that be in sentiment, sales, engagement, behaviour or actions – that meets essential key objectives.

articleTitle: The eccentric engineer: Statistics the many, varied and unappreciated careers of William Playfair: The story of an adventurous and revolutionary engineer, draughtsman, inventor, silversmith, merchant, banker, statistician, pamphleteer, editor, speculator… and convict
abstract: NOT MANY children who grapple with pie charts, bar charts and time-series plots know they can thank an engineer for their misery. Nor would William Playfair have probably wanted to be remembered as such – but few can choose where fate takes them, and Playfair was taken further than many.

articleTitle: Thinking cap: A mathematician's notebook, timing a burning rope and tripling numbers are all tricky puzzles for you to figure out this month, with a chance of a prize for the correct answer
abstract: PUZZLE 1: DISAPPEARING NUMBERS: The page below is from a mathematician's notebook. The last grid of numbers at the bottom right has been torn from the page. Can you work out all the numbers that the last grid contained?

articleTitle: Tanks, graves, mirrors and antennas: We announce the results of E&T's Hidden engineering Heritage competition
abstract: AT LAST, TIME HAS COME to sum up our ‘Hidden Engineering Heritage’ (HEH) Competition. It took us the best part of last year to collect the entries and to judge them. Why so long? The answer is in the first part of the competition's name — ‘Hidden’. Something that has been truly ‘hidden’ takes time to spot, let alone photograph and describe. As is always the case with our competitions, we were after quality rather than quantity, and quality entries take time. That was why we eventually decided to extend the final deadline by a couple of months.

articleTitle: Book Interview: Destination Red Planet (probably) and (maybe) beyond…: Half a century has passed since Nasa's Apollo programme first put humans on the Moon. And we haven't been back since. But all that is set to change in the coming decades, says David Whitehouse in his new book ‘Space 2069‘

The measure of 19C-1E electric excavator: In July 2020, JCB's 19C-1E electric digger scooped one of the world's most prestigious prizes for engineering innovation – the UK's Royal Academy of Engineering MacRobert Award
abstract: IN WINNING THE 2020 MacRobert Award, JCB faced strong competition from two other shortlisted finalists: the all-electric I-PACE sports utility vehicle from Jaguar Land Rover and ecoSMRT liquid natural gas reliquification technology from Babcock's LGE business.

articleTitle: Eu plans for future resilience: Europe's energy system has proved up to the task of dealing with the coronavirus outbreak but the sector's future is at the mercy of volatile and unpredictable factors. Kadri Simson, EU Energy Commissioner, tells E&T that fundamental changes are needed to protect the roll out of clean power and prevent a greenhouse gas rebound
abstract: VIRUS LOCKDOWN measures and shuttered industries are predicted to slash global emission levels by 8 per cent this year, according to the International Energy Agency, while a reduced demand for electricity has boosted the standing of renewable energy sources.

articleTitle: Finance high-tech cash machines could replace physical bank branches
abstract: WITH THE number of cash transactions dwindling rapidly in the wake of the coronavirus lockdown, one of the world's largest cash machine manufacturers has called for the implementation of new technologies to ensure that those who still rely on paper money will continue to have access to it.

articleTitle: Words and portrait by Nick Smith: As the Eden Project celebrates its 20th anniversary, its CEO and thought leader Sir Tim Smit reflects on the technological achievement and educational impact of simulating rainforest and Mediterranean climates in a clay pit in rural Cornwall
abstract: “IF YOU WANT to know anything about the way I think,” say Sir Tim Smit, “this is where you need to start.” He casts an expansive and proprietorial arm gesture around a dingy, cluttered office not much bigger than a rabbit hutch. There's something eccentric about his office environment that doesn't seem to stack up against the classic image of the CEO.

articleTitle: Interview Miles Adcock
abstract: “MY JOB TITLE is probably the most fantastic one in the world,” says Miles Adcock, president of space and quantum at Teledyne e2v, a UK-based company that produces imaging sensors for applications that are literally out of this world. There's also more down-to-earth technology being manufactured at the company's Chelmsford facility in Essex, but “today, one of the largest projects we're working on is PLATO” (Planetary Transits and Oscillations of stars), part of the European Space Agency (ESA) Cosmic Vision programme. “We'll be delivering 126 sensors onto 26 satellites, which will go into space to detect planets that have the potential for hosting Earth-like lifeforms.”

articleTitle: Policing time to tackl taser misuse
abstract: IN FEBRUARY, after a car crash in Birmingham, Trevaile Wyse, a black man who says he was an innocent bystander, was tasered by a West Midlands Police (WMP) officer. A video of the incident shows Wyse tasered at close range. The officer, standing less than three metres away, directs the conducted energy device (CED) towards Wyse's throat. It's where the upper dart pierces him, with the other in his chest. Later, Wyse described being tasered as bad, “[but] being tasered in the throat is ten times worse”.

articleTitle: Innovate and celebrate: A virtual celebration of some very real winners will take place on 19 November 2020. What's more – you're invited!
abstract: While the black ties and cocktail dresses may remain in the wardrobe for this year's E&T Innovation Awards, the change in circumstances opens up the event to the entire engineering and technology community. This year, everyone is invited. For free. All you need to do is register (go to eandt.theiet.org/innovation).

articleTitle: In the market for virus prevention: With the coronavirus pandemic still raging, scientists are trying to discover how toxic pathogens move from animals to humans. But until the global wildlife trade is regulated, or better still banned, it is unlikely that Covid-19 will be the last deadly pathogen to emerge from the natural world
abstract: TOWARDS THE END of April, the US National Institutes of Health (NIH), a medical research centre and agency of the US Department of Health and Human Services, abruptly terminated a multimillion dollar grant that would have paid for four years of research into how coronaviruses move from bats to humans, in the part of the world where the current pandemic started.

articleTitle: The Graphic AI cyber-bullying detection: E&T tested whether detection of toxic content on social media can be automated. The results suggest technology still has a long way to go
abstract: BILLIONS OF messages are sent to social media networks every day, which makes the work of content curators tough.

articleTitle: Book reviews spacefarers, the alchemy of us, qualityland: Harvard university press spacefarers: How humans will settle the moon, mars and beyond: Colonising other planets, how materials have changed the way we live, and a fictional dystopia run on algorithms
abstract: BY CHRISTOPHER WANJEK, £23.95, ISBN 9780674984486: Now that celebrations surrounding the 50th anniversary of the Apollo 11 mission are over, space-minded authors have pivoted back towards the decades-old question of why no one has returned to the Moon for so long. To his credit, Christopher Wanjek doesn't waste too many words on the answer; it's simply a matter of high costs, poor decisions and the fact that it really is ‘rocket science’.

articleTitle: Book reviews: You look like a thing and I love you, find your path, Mallard
abstract: AI is usually characterised as a faceless, mysterious, all-powerful entity that is going to steal all ourjobs/create a utopia/render us disposable and perhaps kill us all. Really, AI is already here and changing our world. This book is a short and sweet guide to what AI is, how it works, what it can do and, importantly, what it can't do.

articleTitle: The graphic: Where London builds: Data released by CTBUH shows where London's recent building boom has had most impact. Skyscrapers became an essential feature in housing Londoners, especially those at the young and poor end
abstract: WHEN 30 ST MARY AXE, or ‘The Gherkin’ was finally completed in 2003, soaring 180m into the sky, it was one of the tallest buildings in London. Today it is barely visible among the surrounding skyscrapers, and has slipped to 13th in the ‘tallest’ chart. Internationally, London ranks far behind other cities now: 50th place in terms of buildings over 150m according to data from the Global Tall Building Database from the CTBUH (Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat).

articleTitle: Words and portrait by nick smith: Simon Maskell a data scientist at the University of Liverpool, discusses his current work on a data system to support the UK government's response to Covid-19. “I don't see data as a quest for truth: I see it as a tool for making decisions,” he says
abstract: WHEN IT COMES to the way in which Covid-19 mortality data is presented in the media – or any other data related to spread of infection, transport usage or international comparisons – the trouble is that “while you are looking at very clear numbers, it's not exactly clear what those numbers mean”. These are the words of Simon Maskell, data scientist at the University of Liverpool or, to give him his full job title, which he admits is “not particularly snappy”, Professor of Autonomous Systems in the School of Electrical Engineering, Electronics and Computer Science. Whichever way you choose to describe what he does, he's an acknowledged academic expert in the field of data science. Only don't call him ‘professor’ or ‘doctor’. “Simon will do. I don't go in for all that hierarchical management stuff.”

articleTitle: Book reviews quantum legacies, samsung rising, the future we choose: University of chicago press quantum legacies: Dispatches from an uncertain world: Science in a social context, how a tech giant established itself, and an inside take on the Paris Climate Accord
abstract: BY DAVID KAISER, £21, ISBN 9780226698052: For more than a century, scientists have been pitting their wits against the conceptual uncertainties of quantum theory, trying to make sense of a messy world in which cats can be famously alive and dead at the same time (providing they're in a box) and some particles tunnel through walls while others share entangled fates.

articleTitle: The measure of X-59 quiet SuperSonic technology (QueSST) X-plane
abstract: DESIGNED BY AEROSPACE and defence company Lockheed Martin, the X-59 Quiet SuperSonic Technology (QueSST) aircraft is Nasa's first large-scale, piloted X-plane (or experimental aircraft) in more than three decades.

articleTitle: Facial-recognition system for remote id verification wins africa prize
abstract: A 26-YEAR-OLD ENGINEER has won the Royal Academy of Engineering's 2020 Africa Prize for Engineering Innovation, after developing software that allows businesses to use facial recognition for online identity verification. Charlette N'Guessan is the first woman to win the prestigious prize since it was established in 2014, and the first winner from Ghana.

articleTitle: The EV life-cycle conundrum: How well do electric vehicles stack up against their counterparts when you take all the inputs into account?
abstract: A SEMINAL ANALYSIS of the environmental cost of cars turns 20 this autumn. In ‘On The Road In 2020: A life-cycle analysis of new automobile technologies’, the late Malcolm Weiss and colleagues from the Energy Laboratory at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology calculated how much it takes not just to keep a car on the road but to put it there in the first place. Written as Al Gore turned his attention from a failed presidential campaign to warning of climate change, the report focused on the greenhouse gas emissions from conventional and future automotive technologies.

articleTitle: Materials: Hot on the trail of the ultracold: Wolfgang Ketterle is an expert in the weird world of ultracold atoms. E&T spoke to him about the phenomena and technologies only possible near absolute zero, and his fears for a fractured, anti-scientific world
abstract: THE WORLD IS full of noise; the most serene scenes are abuzz with moving atoms. Under certain extraordinary conditions, however, these atoms can be frozen in their tracks.

articleTitle: CSI… can't believe it! the weirdest ways crimes have been solved: Better than a delicious plot twist in a crime novel that's both shocking and satisfying, some real-life crimes have been solved in the strangest of ways. In fact, some are so bizarre that they may seem like the cunning concoctions by Arthur Conan Doyle
abstract: IN MODERN TIMES, baffling crimes are seldom solved by an eccentric genius like Sherlock Holmes. More commonly the critical discoveries come from teams of specialists called upon by the police.

articleTitle: Recycle our grandparents' ideas and make a difference: Nostalgia for Britain in the middle of the last century has put the spotlight on some habits and choices that could hold the key to reducing our individual carbon footprint by 2050
abstract: THERE was a noticeable ‘reset’ for the environment during this pandemic's early lockdown. As well as less traffic on the roads, reduced noise and air pollution, we saw people looking to local, community-based pastimes, such as baking and gardening.

articleTitle: WHat?! I Can't hear you!
abstract: The biggest clamours most of us will experience are things like fire alarms and jet engines - but the loudest noises in existence would do far worse than make you wince. Here are some of the most ear-shattering sounds ever recorded.

articleTitle: The graphic: Climate change patent boom: Despite being the largest carbon emitter in the world, China produces vastly more patents related to climate change than all other major patent offices
GCHQ: The story so far: As the first ever authorised history of Britain's secretive cyber-intelligence agency GCHQ hits the bookshops, we talk to its author John Ferris
abstract: IT'S TEMPTING TO slip into journalistic clichés about signals intelligence (or ‘Sigint’) being a ‘shadowy world shrouded in cloak-and-dagger intrigue’. And it's, no doubt, attractive to the headline writer to use sensational vocabulary – such as the inevitable ‘lifting the lid’ – to get the reader's attention. But neither will be the most helpful approach to understanding John Ferris's balanced account of the century-long history of the UK's Government Communications Headquarters, GCHQ, the first to be written with the full cooperation of the organisation.

articleTitle: Words and portrait by nick smith: Kaarel Kotkas is a 25-year-old Estonian entrepreneur, whose online identity verification start-up Veriff is forecast to be the next tech unicorn' or billion-dollar company. Here, he discusses how Veriff tackles ID fraud in the cyber world
abstract: IT ALL DEPENDS on what figures you go to, but most sources agree that cyber crime is one of the biggest global threats facing us today. To take one estimate, Cybersecurity Ventures predicts global cyber crime will be worth $6tn annually by next year. If anywhere near correct, we now have a criminal enterprise on our hands, bigger than the entire worldwide illegal drug trade and the largest collective financial transaction in the history of humanity. Whichever source you go to, as Kaarel Kotkas says, cyber crime is “pretty big and we're seeing the problem of establishing identity on a scale previously unseen”. His company, Veriff, is aiming to play a role in combating online fraud, especially in the banking sector.

articleTitle: The gallery: Nasa's space launch system
abstract: NASA has shown off the completed core section of its first SLS super-heavy-lift rocket. The huge Space Launch System core was wheeled out of Nasa's Michoud Assembly Facility in New Orleans last month for transfer by barge to a test site in Mississippi. The SLS will play a crucial role in Nasa's Artemis programme, which aims to return humans to the Moon by 2024.

articleTitle: BookInterview: All we hear is radium gaga: Radium has only been with us for just over a century, but its impact on our lives has ranged from the sublime to the ridiculous. Author of ‘Half Lives’ Lucy Jane Santos finds herself in her element
abstract: “IT'S THE commercial and entertainment side of radium that sets it aside from anything else,” says Lucy Jane Santos. She's describing how the early 20th-century public and medical establishment both embraced a newly discovered and highly dangerous radioactive element in the hope that it would replace surgery, while literally lighting up theatrical costumes, watch dials and cocktails.

articleTitle: Thinking cap: Squared triangles, millions of grains and a rope around the Earth are the topics for this month's testing puzzles, with a chance of a great prize for the correct answer
abstract: PUZZLE 1 TRIANGLES THAT ARE SQUARES: Jack and his elder sister Jill liked playing with round counters. Jack proudly constructed a perfect six by six square using 36 red counters, as shown:

articleTitle: Technology ai techniques boost battery lifespan and safety
abstract: MACHINE LEARNING could be used to predict the health of a battery with 10 times greater accuracy than the current industry standard, according to UK researchers behind a new method which demonstrates this.

articleTitle: The graphic bad air around covid-19: How resuming pollution levels after the lockdown could affect a second wave of coronavirus patients
abstract: The world feels emptier under lockdown. Traffic is down. Coal and oil burning is down. All this helps to clean up the air. “It offers a glimpse of what the air will be like in the near future when the transition to clean energy is further along,” says Lauri Myllyvirta from the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA). But what comes after the lockdown remains uncertain.
